prompt: Why do ethers often show a strong fragment from α-cleavage next to the oxygen?

options.label: α-cleavage gives an oxocarbenium ion (R-O⁺=CHR'), stabilized by O's lone pair
The C–O bond is much weaker than C-C, so it breaks preferentially
Ethers rearrange to 3-membered oxiranes before ionizing, giving the ring-opened fragment
Ethers lose water in MS the way alcohols do, giving an M-18 base peak

explanation: α-cleavage next to the ether O gives a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion (R-O⁺=CHR' ↔ R-O-CHR'⁺) — much more stable than a plain alkyl cation. Diagnostic for ethers. The C-O bond is actually comparable in strength to C-C; the driver is cation stability of the product, not bond weakness.
